'''''Calycanthus floridus''''', or commonly known as the '''eastern sweetshrub''', '''Carolina allspice''', or '''spicebush''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/calycanthus-floridus/|title=''Calycanthus floridus'' (Bubby Bush, Carolina Allspice, Common Sweetshrub, Spicebush, Sweet Betsy, Sweet Bubby Bush, Sweetshrub, Sweet Shrub) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu|access-date=2020-04-03}}</ref> is a species of flowering shrub in the family [[Calycanthaceae]].<ref>{{Cite PLANTS|symbol=CAFL22|taxon=Calycanthus floridus|access-date=2020-04-03}}</ref> It is identifiable by its dark red flowers and fragrant scent. It is non-invasive and is found in the Southeastern United States. The Nature Conservancy considers its conservation status to be [[NatureServe conservation status|G5]], globally secure, indicating it is at low risk of extinction.<ref name=ns/>

==Description==
''Calycanthus floridus'' is a shrub that grows to be around {{cvt|6 to 9|ft|0}} tall.{{r|mobotpf}} Its leaves are a dark green with a pale underside. They are ovate or elliptical in shape and grow to be about {{convert|6|in|cm}} in length.{{r|mobotpf}} The leaves are simple, entire, and arranged oppositely along the stem.<ref name=mortonarb>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mortonarb.org/trees-plants/tree-plant-descriptions/carolina-allspice|title=Carolina allspice|website=www.mortonarb.org|access-date=2020-04-19}}</ref>

The flowers are solitary, featuring a reddish brown to reddish purple color when they bloom in spring. They are aromatic and so are the leaves when bruised.{{r|mobotpf}} The flowers have a [[hypanthium]] that is more than {{cvt|2|cm|1}} long.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Radford, Albert E.|title=Manual of the vascular flora of the Carolinas|date=1968|publisher=University of North Carolina Press|others=Ahles, Harry E.,, Bell, C. Ritchie|isbn=0-8078-1087-8|location=Chapel Hill|oclc=355003}}</ref> The shape of the flowers can be cylindrical, ellipsoid, pyriform, or globose.{{r|fna}} The flowers have numerous [[Tepal|tepals]] that can either be oblong-elliptic or obovate-lanceolate at maturity.{{r|fna}} The flowers are [[Plant reproductive morphology|perfect]], having both [[Stamen|stamens]] and [[Gynoecium|carpels]] on the flowers. The [[Stamen|stamens]] are numerous, connective beyond the anthers.<ref name=":1" /> The [[Gynoecium|carpels]] are numerous. They are free, with a single ovary in a [[locule]].<ref name=":1" />

The fruits are [[Dehiscence (botany)|indehiscent]] [[Pseudocarp|pseudocarps]] that are about {{cvt|8|cm|0}} in length and {{cvt|5|cm|0}} in diameter at maturity.<ref name=":1" /> They are formed within the receptacle and contain numerous [[Achene|achenes]] that are roughly {{cvt|10|mm|1}} long with a {{cvt|5|mm|1}} diameter.

==Taxonomy==
[[File:The natural history of Carolina, Florida, and the Bahama Islands, 1754 Garrulus Carolinensis - The Chatterer (19117862074) rev.jpg|thumb|Oldest illustration, from a work by [[Mark Catesby]] published from 1731 onwards]]
''Calycanthus floridus'' was first scientifically described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1759.<ref name=IPNI_139221-1/> It was the only species in his new genus ''Calycanthus''. Linnaeus referred to an earlier illustration by [[Mark Catesby]],<ref name=Linn59/> contained in a work published from 1731 onwards.

==Distribution and habitat==
''Calycanthus floridus'' is native to the eastern United States.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=cafl22|title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin|website=www.wildflower.org|access-date=2020-04-20}}</ref> It is presumed to have been [[extirpated]] from Ohio.<ref name=ns/> It prefers sunny habitats but can tolerate moderate amounts of shade. It grows well in environments that feature moist substrate.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/plants/calycanthus-floridus|title=Calycanthus floridus {{!}} Landscape Plants {{!}} Oregon State University|website=landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu|access-date=2020-04-20}}</ref> 

==Uses==
It is used in horticulture as the flowers are showy and fragrant.<ref name=":4" /> The bark of the plant is edible and is reportedly used as a substitute for [[cinnamon]]. The petals of the flower are also reportedly used in medicinal tea-making. Strong caution is advised however, as an [[alkaloid]] in the plant may lead to heart convulsions. The viscous substance within the plant is reportedly used as a disinfectant.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Calycanthus+floridus|title=''Calycanthus floridus'', Carolina Allspice, Eastern sweetshrub, Strawberry Bush, Sweetshrub, Carolina Allspice PFAF Plant Database|website=pfaf.org|access-date=2020-04-20}}</ref>

It is highly resistant to diseases and insects, although it is prone to infection by ''[[Agrobacterium tumefaciens]]'', which leads to the formation of [[crown gall]]s on the stems.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fp095|title=''Calycanthus floridus'', Carolina Allspice, Sweetshrub|last=Gilman|first=Edward|date=27 May 2015|website=EDIS|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080318134953/http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu:80/FP095 |archive-date=18 March 2008 |access-date=April 16, 2020}}</ref>

This plant has been marked as a pollinator plant, supporting and attracting beetles.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Planting Guides|url=https://www.pollinator.org/pollinator.org/assets/generalFiles/OzarkBroadleafrx1FINAL_171017_085901.pdf|access-date=2022-01-29|website=Pollinator.org|language=en-US}}</ref>
